_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-14) story fix: the new labels start tonight, so no earlier id clashes
title: Proof

post.author: u/fridge_two_ksenia
post.title: I'm the night technician at a toxicology lab. At 23:40 our records put one blood sample in two cases. I'm holding the tube. It has one label.

blocks.text: Fenwold Toxicology Laboratory tests blood and urine for drugs and poisons, for the police and the coroner. That work is called toxicology. I'm the night technician: I receive the tubes and put them in the fridges.

Every tube needs an unbroken record of who held it, when, and for which case. That record is called the chain of custody. If it breaks, a court can throw the result out, like a receipt with a page torn away.
Each tube has a label with a pattern of stripes that a scanner reads as digits. The stripes are a barcode. The digits are the tube's sample id: its number in our records.

Old labels have 8 digits: the date as year, month and day, then a 2-digit count. 26100510 is 5 October 2026, sample 10. On the evening of Monday 5 October, half our benches switched to new scanners and 9-digit labels: the date, then a 3-digit count starting at 100, "so the two kinds can never clash". The old benches kept going until their rolls ran out.
Our evidence-tracking service is the program that keeps the chain of custody. Wolfram, our computer person, wrote it in Python, a language for writing programs.

When I scan a tube, the service goes in steps. First it takes the digits the scanner sends. Then a small part of it cuts the sample id out of those digits. That part is called the parser. Last, it files the tube under that id, with its case.

Wolfram also wrote small checks. Each gives one piece of the code an input, runs that piece alone, and compares the answer with the right one, like testing one cog of a clock on the bench. Each check is called a unit test.
His unit tests never touch a real scanner. They use a stand-in, written in code, that answers the way its author decided. That stand-in is called a fake.
Here is the code. def sample_id(raw) starts a function, a named set of steps, given the raw digits. raw[:8] means the first 8 characters, and # starts a note.
FakeScanner is a class, a pattern for a kind of thing in code. Its read() always gives back the same 8 digits:

def sample_id(raw):
    return raw[:8]              # ids are 8 digits

class FakeScanner:              # used by every unit test
    def read(self): return "26100514"
All 12 unit tests passed. His report gave the coverage: the share of the code's lines the tests ran. It was 70%, 14 of the service's 20 lines.
At 21:12 I scanned an old label, 26100510, a blood tube for case 3307, and put it in fridge 2. The old roll ran out at 23:16, on 26100518.

At 23:40 a courier brought the night's first new-label tubes: three for case 3313. I scanned the first, a blood tube: 261005100. The screen showed its record. Each line shows the id, the time received, the case and the tube:
Case 3307's tube is in fridge 2. The tube in my hand says 261005100. The other two, 261005101 and 261005102, landed on 26100510 too.
I've set the three tubes aside, each with a note. What should Wolfram change before tomorrow night?

The new label 261005100, received at 23:40 for case 3313, also comes out as 26100510, because the parser keeps the first 8 characters. Both land on one record, 26100510, which now holds case 3307 at 21:12 and case 3313 at 23:40.

The new label 261005100, the day's first, went in at 23:40 for case 3313, lost its last digit in the parser, and landed on the same record. The other two new tubes, 261005101 and 261005102, landed there too.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Wolfram's unit tests did what unit tests do: they checked the parser alone, with the input the test gave it. A test that runs several real parts together, say the real scanner, the parser and the records, is called an integration test. It's slower, and it catches what the parts get wrong about each other. There's a narrower kind for the edge where your code meets a machine you didn't build: you record what the real machine actually sends, then check your code against those recordings. That's a contract test, like trying a key in the real lock instead of against a drawing of the key. So, questions. Which ids did any test ever send the parser? What does each real scanner send? And is 26100510 the only old id the new labels could land on?

replies.author: u/fridge_two_ksenia
replies.text: Wolfram checked. Every test sent the parser 26100514, from the fake. The old scanner sends 8 digits and the new one 9, and he has recordings from both. The scanner company says a third model, due in the spring, will print 10 digits. He also says a full run through his test copy of the lab system takes about 4 minutes a sample.

comments.author: u/ninety_five_gisbert
comments.text: Your coverage is the real problem. 70% means almost a third of that service never ran in a test, and bugs live in the code nobody ran. Get it to 95% and make every line earn its place. I've run teams that wouldn't accept a change under 90%, and this kind of thing didn't happen to us.

comments.author: u/whole_lab_swanhild
comments.text: Unit tests with a fake prove the fake works. Test the way a tube really travels: scan it, file it, test it, and check the report lands in the right case, through the whole lab system. A test that runs the work from one end to the other like that is called an end-to-end test. Slow, yes, but it's the only test that sees what a court sees.

reply.prompt: Tomorrow night both kinds of label will be scanned again. What should Wolfram change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Change the fake scanner to send 9-digit ids, so the unit tests match the new scanners.
options.verdict: Right for today, blind to the next change
options.part2: Wolfram changed FakeScanner to send 261005100. One unit test failed at once, 11 of 12, because the parser gave back 26100510. He changed the parser to keep the first 9 characters, raw[:9], and all 12 passed again. Replayed, the evening was clean: 12 ids on file, none in two cases. But the fake still knew only what Wolfram told it. In the spring the third scanner arrived with 10-digit labels. On the bench, its first label, 2704121000, came out as 270412100: the id the 9-digit label for that day's sample 100 carries. The unit tests stayed green, because the fake had never sent 10 digits.
options.senior: Changing the fake moves its author's guess from 8 digits to 9; it is still a guess. The tests now agree with the scanners you have, until the next one. A fake only knows what its author assumed, so it can't tell you when the real machine changes. And the parser still trims: it just trims one place later. Nothing in the tests checks the fake against a real scanner.

options.text: Add a contract test that feeds real scanners' ids to the parser, and keep each id whole.
options.part2: Wolfram changed the parser to keep each id whole: an 8- or 9-digit id is filed exactly as read, and any other length is refused and the tube set aside for a person. Then he added contract tests: four recorded reads from the real scanners, 26100514 and 26100509 from the old model, 261005100 and 261005101 from the new. On the old parser only 2 of 4 passed: both new reads came back as 26100510. On the new one, 4 of 4, in 0.20 seconds. Replayed, the evening had 12 ids on file and none in two cases. In the spring the scanner company sent recordings from the 10-digit model before it arrived. Added to the contract tests, 4 of 6 passed: both spring reads were refused. The tests went red before that scanner reached a bench, and Wolfram changed the parser for it on purpose.
options.senior: A contract test checks the fake's guess against the real machine: record what each real scanner sends and run the parser on it, every time the code changes. Keeping the id whole means a new format can't quietly turn into an old one, and refusing a length no scanner sends makes the surprise loud instead of silent. The costs: someone must keep the recordings current as scanners change, and a refused tube waits for a person.

options.text: Add end-to-end tests that take a sample from scanning to report through the whole lab system.
options.verdict: Real and useful, and it missed
options.part2: Wolfram added two end-to-end tests: one old label, 26100501, and one new, 261005100, each scanned, filed, tested and reported in his test copy of the lab system. They passed, 2 of 2, in 8 minutes. 261005100 became 26100510, but no test sample was 26100510, so nothing clashed, and the first-8 parser stayed. Replayed, the evening still put 26100510 in case 3307 and case 3313. Only when he tried a pair that clash, 26100510 and 261005100, did the end-to-end tests go red: 0 of 2.
options.senior: End-to-end tests are worth having: they check the whole path a tube takes, the way a court would. But they are slow, about 4 minutes a sample here, so you can only afford a few, and a few samples catch a clash only if one of them happens to collide. Keep a handful for the main paths, and catch format problems lower down, where tests are fast enough to try every kind of input.

options.text: Raise unit test coverage from 70% to 95%, so every line of the service has a test of its own.
options.verdict: More lines run, the same one input
options.part2: Wolfram wrote 9 more unit tests: 21 in all, running 19 of the 20 lines, 95% coverage. All 21 passed, in 0.42 seconds. Every new test still used the fake, so every test still sent 26100514. Replayed, the evening was the same: 9 ids on file, 3 tubes under a wrong id, and 26100510 holding case 3307 and case 3313.
options.senior: Coverage counts the lines a test ran, not the inputs it tried. raw[:8] was run by the first test ever written, so it was already covered: right for 8 digits, wrong for 9. 95% coverage with one fake input proves the code works for that one input. Coverage is good for finding code no test touches at all, not for proving the tests ask the right questions.

sim.title: Replay the evening at Fenwold, and test the parser
sim.lede: You're Wolfram, replaying Monday 5 October 2026 from 21:00, before the first scan. Twelve tubes come in: old 8-digit labels 26100510 (21:12, case 3307, blood) through 26100518 (23:16, the last on the old roll), then one courier run at 23:40 for case 3313 with the day's first three new 9-digit labels, 261005100, 261005101 and 261005102. Pick the parser: the first 8 characters, as built; the first 9; or the whole id, refusing any length but 8 or 9. Pick which tests run. Unit tests all use FakeScanner: 12 tests at 70% coverage as built, or 21 at 95% (coverage is counted on the 20-line service as built); the fake can send 26100514 or 261005100. Contract tests run the parser on recorded reads from the real scanners: 26100514 and 26100509 from the old model, 261005100 and 261005101 from the new, and if you add them, 2704121000 and 2704121004 from the planned 10-digit spring model (2704121000 is 12 April 2027, sample 1000; 270412100 would be that day's 9-digit sample 100). End-to-end tests take about 4 minutes a sample, on 26100501 and 261005100, or on a clashing pair, 26100510 and 261005100. The bench tries one scanner at a time. Changing the parser rewinds to 21:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Run to 23:40 as built: 261005100 is filed as 26100510, which now holds case 3307 and case 3313. 9 ids on file, 3 tubes under a wrong id, 1 id holding two cases. Run the tests: unit 12 of 12, green, 70%, 0.24 seconds (shown as 0.24 s). Raise coverage to 95%: 21 of 21, still green, still wrong. Turn on end-to-end: 2 of 2 in 8 minutes; only the clashing pair goes red, 0 of 2. Turn on contract tests: 2 of 4, red. Pick the whole id: 12 ids, none in two cases, contract 4 of 4. Add the spring model: 4 of 6, both refused. Then make the fake send 9 digits: 11 of 12 with first 8, 12 of 12 with first 9, and the bench turns 2704121000 into 270412100.

explain.oneLine: Nobody moved the tube. The parser kept the first 8 characters of every id, so 261005100 was filed as 26100510, an old sample from another case. Every test passed because every test used a fake that sent 8 digits, and no test ever asked what a real new scanner sends. The fix is to check the parser against recordings from the real scanners, and to keep each id whole, refusing any length no scanner sends.

steps.title: Unit tests check one piece alone.
steps.text: A unit test goes in steps. First, it sets up an input, written into the test. Next, it runs one piece of code, here sample_id(), on that input, with nothing else real around it. Then it compares the answer with the expected one and passes or fails. Unit tests are fast, about 0.02 seconds each here, so you can have hundreds and run them on every change. What can go wrong: the test only tries the inputs its author thought of. Every one of Wolfram's 12 tests gave the parser 26100514, so raw[:8] was right every time. The tests were true; they were just about a world with one kind of label.

steps.title: A fake knows only what its author assumed.
steps.text: Anything that stands in for a real part during a test is a test double. A fake is a working stand-in that takes a shortcut, like FakeScanner returning one fixed id. A mock is a stand-in that also checks it was called the way the test expected. Doubles make tests fast and repeatable, and they hide one thing: whether the real part still behaves like the double. When the lab bought new scanners, the real part changed and the fake didn't. Changing the fake to send 9 digits only swaps one guess for another.

steps.title: Bigger tests: more real parts, fewer tests.
steps.text: An integration test runs several real parts together, such as a real scanner, the parser and the records, and catches what they get wrong about each other. An end-to-end test runs the whole path: scan, file, test the blood, report to the case. Each is slower and breaks more easily than the one below, so the usual advice is a test pyramid: many small unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle, a few end-to-end tests at the top. Here, 2 end-to-end samples took 8 minutes and passed, because neither of them happened to collide with the other.

steps.title: Contract tests check the edge.
steps.text: Where your code meets a machine or a company you don't control, a contract test checks your code against what that machine really sends. It goes in steps. First, record real reads from each scanner model. Next, run the parser on every recording. Then check that each id comes back exactly as read. Run them on every change, and record again whenever a scanner, its software or its labels change. On the first-8 parser they fail at once, 2 of 4: 261005100 and 261005101 both come back as 26100510. What can go wrong: the recordings go stale, and the tests stay green for a scanner that no longer behaves that way.

steps.title: Keep the id whole; refuse what no scanner sends.
steps.text: raw[:8] made every input fit, and that is the danger: cutting input to shape turns a surprise into a wrong record. Checking input against the rules and refusing what breaks them is called validation. The fixed parser keeps an 8- or 9-digit id exactly as read, so 261005100 and 26100510 are different samples, and refuses any other length, so a tube is set aside for a person instead of filed under someone else's id. Replayed, the evening has 12 ids and none in two cases, and the spring model's 10 digits are refused before its first night.

diagram.aria: The fix. Recorded reads from the old and new scanners, 26100514, 26100509, 261005100 and 261005101, feed the contract tests and the parser, which keeps each id whole: 4 of 4 pass, and the evening files 12 ids with none in two cases. The spring model's 2704121000 has 10 digits, so the parser refuses it and the tube is set aside.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tomorrow night. Contract tests run the parser on recorded reads from both real scanners, and all 4 pass because each id is kept whole. Replayed in the sim, the evening files 12 ids, none in two cases. The spring model's 10-digit labels are refused, so its contract tests go red before it reaches a bench.

fix.title: The fix: contract tests on real reads, and whole ids
fix.text: Change sample_id() to keep the id whole: if it is 8 or 9 digits, return it exactly as read; otherwise refuse it, so the service sets the tube aside and tells the technician. Keep the unit tests with FakeScanner; they are still fast and still useful for the logic. Add contract tests: record reads from every scanner model in use, 26100514 and 26100509 from the old one and 261005100 and 261005101 from the new, and check that the parser gives each back unchanged. Run them on every change, and ask for recordings from any new model before it arrives. Keep two or three end-to-end tests for the main path, and include one pair of ids that would clash under any cut. Then repair tonight's record by hand: split 26100510 into case 3307's tube and the three case 3313 tubes, with a note in the chain of custody saying why. In the sim: 12 ids, 0 in two cases, contract 4 of 4.

limits: Contract tests are only as fresh as their recordings. If a scanner's software changes and nobody records it again, the tests stay green for a machine that no longer behaves that way.
Refusing a length no scanner sends is loud, and loud has a cost: a refused tube waits for a person at night, and the night technician needs a clear step for what to do with it.
A contract test checks the format, not the meaning. A scanner that misreads one digit sends a valid 9-digit id, and only the label, a person or a check digit on the label can catch that.

explain.seniorTake: A test proves what it tries, nothing more. Unit tests with fakes are the cheap, fast base of the pyramid, and they should stay; but every fake is a guess about a machine you don't control, and the guess goes out of date the day the machine changes. So check the guess where the two meet: record what the real machine sends and run your code on it, and record again whenever that machine changes. And, as a rule, don't cut input to make it fit. A value you don't recognise is news; keep it whole, or refuse it loudly, and let a person decide. Coverage tells you which lines ran, not which inputs were tried, and end-to-end tests are too slow to try many.

realWorld.title: Ariane 5 flight 501, 1996: about 40 seconds
realWorld.text: The Inquiry Board's report opens: "On 4 June 1996, the maiden flight of the Ariane 5 launcher ended in a failure." It came "Only about 40 seconds after initiation of the flight sequence". The cause was in the inertial reference system, the SRI, which the report says was reused: "The design of the Ariane 5 SRI is practically the same as that of an SRI which is presently used on Ariane 4".

realWorld.title: Ariane 501: a number too big for its box
realWorld.text: The report says: "The floating point number which was converted had a value greater than what could be represented by a 16-bit signed integer." The conversion had been left unprotected on the assumption "that they were either physically limited or that there was a large margin of safety".

realWorld.title: Ariane 501: a new rocket, a new range
realWorld.text: The value was the horizontal bias, BH, and "The value of BH was much higher than expected" because "the early part of the trajectory of Ariane 5 differs from that of Ariane 4". The trajectory is the path the rocket flies.

realWorld.title: Ariane 501: the new rocket's data was never tried
realWorld.text: The report says "it was jointly agreed not to include the Ariane 5 trajectory data in the SRI requirements and specification", and that "no test was performed to verify that the SRI would behave correctly" in the new rocket's conditions. Its recommendations include: "Identify all implicit assumptions made by the code and its justification documents", and "Prepare a test facility including as much real equipment as technically feasible".

realWorld.title: Fowler, 2012: the test pyramid
realWorld.text: Martin Fowler writes that the test pyramid's "essential point is that you should have many more low-level UnitTests than high level BroadStackTests". On the top of the pyramid: "In short, tests that run end-to-end through the UI are: brittle, expensive to write, and time consuming to run." The UI, short for user interface, is the screens a person uses, and broad-stack tests are tests that run through many layers of a system at once.

realWorld.title: Fowler, 2011: contract tests
realWorld.text: Fowler describes the question a contract test answers: "whether the double is indeed an accurate representation of the external service". The tests "check that all the calls against your test doubles return the same results as a call to the external service would." And: "Contract tests check the contract of external service calls, but not necessarily the exact data."

realWorld.title: Fowler, 2006: test doubles, fakes and mocks
realWorld.text: "Test Double is a generic term for any case where you replace a production object for testing purposes." Of fakes: "Fake objects actually have working implementations, but usually take some shortcut". Of mocks: "Mocks are pre-programmed with expectations which form a specification of the calls they are expected to receive."

interview.answer: Both, in different amounts. Unit tests run one piece alone with a fixed input; they are fast, so I want many of them, run on every change. Integration tests run real parts together and catch what the parts get wrong about each other; end-to-end tests run the whole path. Each level up is slower and breaks more easily, so I keep fewer of them: that's the test pyramid. Mocks and fakes lie when the real thing changes and they don't. A fake only knows what its author assumed, so a suite can be green for a format the real system stopped sending. A story I'd tell: a lab's parser kept the first 8 characters of every sample id, and every unit test used a fake scanner that sent 8 digits. New scanners sent 9, the parser cut the last digit off, and a new tube was filed under an old tube's id in another case. Coverage was 70%, and raising it would not have helped, because the line that cut the id was already covered; it had just never seen 9 digits. A contract test is the fix for that gap: record what the real system actually sends, run your code on the recordings on every change, and record again whenever that system changes. And I'd validate input instead of cutting it to fit: keep the id whole, refuse lengths nobody sends, and let a person look at what's refused. Ariane 5's first flight is the famous case: reused code, an assumption about a value's range, never tried on the new rocket's data.

terms.def: The forensic lab in this story. It tests blood and urine for drugs and poisons for the police and the coroner. Its evidence-tracking service was written by Wolfram, in Python.
The study of drugs and poisons in the body. A toxicology lab tests samples such as blood and urine and reports what it found to the case.
The official who looks into sudden or unexplained deaths and may ask a lab to test samples.
The person who receives, checks and stores the tubes overnight at Fenwold. Here, the storyteller.
An unbroken record of who held a piece of evidence, when, and for which case. If it breaks, a court may not trust the result, like a receipt with a page torn away.
A pattern of stripes on a label that a scanner reads as digits.
The digits on a tube's label: its number in the lab's records. Old labels: 8 digits, date then a 2-digit count (26100510). New: 9 digits, date then a count from 100 (261005100).
The program at Fenwold that keeps the chain of custody. When a tube is scanned, it cuts out the sample id and files the tube under that id and its case.
The part of a program that reads raw text and picks out what it needs. Here, sample_id(), which cut the id out of the scanned digits.
A named set of steps in code that takes an input and gives back an answer. In Python it starts with def, as in def sample_id(raw).
Python for the first 8 characters of raw. Given 261005100 it gives 26100510: anything after the eighth character is dropped without a word.
A small check that runs one piece of code on its own with an input written into the test, then compares the answer with the expected one. Fast, so you can have many.
A working stand-in used in tests in place of a real part, taking a shortcut. FakeScanner always returns 26100514, so it only knows what its author assumed.
A stand-in used in tests that is set up in advance with the calls it expects, and checks that the code made them.
Any stand-in that replaces a real part during a test. Fakes, mocks and stubs (stand-ins that just give fixed answers) are all test doubles.
The share of a program's lines that the tests ran at least once. It says which lines ran, not which inputs were tried. Fenwold's was 70%, 14 of 20 lines.
A test that runs several real parts together, such as a real scanner, the parser and the records, to catch what they get wrong about each other. Slower than a unit test.
A test that runs the whole path, here scan, file, test and report, and checks the result where a person would see it. About 4 minutes a sample at Fenwold, so few of them.
A test that checks your code against what a machine or service you don't control really sends, using recordings of it. Like trying a key in the real lock, not a drawing.
A copy of exactly what a real scanner sent for one label, kept for contract tests. Old model: 26100514, 26100509. New model: 261005100, 261005101.
The usual shape of a test suite: many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle, a few slow end-to-end tests at the top.
A set of tests run together. Green means every test in it passed; red means at least one failed.
Checking input against the rules and refusing what breaks them, instead of cutting it to fit. The fixed parser keeps 8- or 9-digit ids whole and refuses any other length.
Python's error for a value that isn't allowed. In the fixed parser, raising it stops the filing step, so the tube is set aside instead of filed.
An id of a length no scanner is known to send. Nothing is filed; the tube is set aside for a person to check.
A third scanner planned for spring 2027, printing 10 digits: date then a count from 1000, such as 2704121000. Its recordings can be added to the contract tests.

terms.term: Tubes under a wrong id (in the sim)
terms.def: Tubes filed under an id different from their label, such as 261005100 filed as 26100510.

terms.term: Ids holding two cases (in the sim)
terms.def: Sample ids whose record lists tubes from more than one case, such as 26100510 with case 3307 and case 3313.
The first flight of Europe's Ariane 5 rocket, on 4 June 1996. It failed about 40 seconds after the flight sequence began, because of an error in reused software.
The rocket's unit that measures its own movement and position. Ariane 5's was practically the same design as Ariane 4's.
The path a rocket flies. Ariane 5's early path differed from Ariane 4's, giving much higher horizontal speeds.
An internal value in the Ariane SRI's alignment software, linked to the rocket's horizontal speed. On Ariane 5 it was much higher than expected.
An extra digit on a label, worked out from the others, so a program can tell when one digit was misread.
The way computers store numbers with a fractional part, across a very wide range of sizes.
A whole number stored in 16 binary digits, so it can only hold values from -32,768 to 32,767. A bigger value doesn't fit.
Fowler's name for a test that runs through many layers of a system at once, such as an end-to-end test.
The screens and buttons a person uses to work a program.
The real system people use, as opposed to a test copy. A production object is the real part a test double stands in for.
The agreed way one program asks another for something and gets an answer, such as a courier company's computers answering your shop's with a price.
The international standard for running information security. A company can be certified against it by an outside auditor. Annex A lists controls, such as A.8.29.

An audit report, under the Trust Services Criteria of the AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants), on how a service company protects its customers' data. CC8.1 is its criterion on changes to systems.

atWork: Look for tests that use a fake or a mock for something outside your code: a partner's API (application programming interface: the agreed way their computers answer yours), a payment provider, an address lookup. It is a common pattern: the partner changes its format, such as prices in pence instead of pounds or a postcode without its space, and every test stays green because the fake still answers the old way. For each such fake, ask when anyone last checked it against the real thing. Record real responses and run your code on them on every change (a contract test), ask partners for samples before they change, and validate what comes in instead of cutting it to fit. Standards, where they apply: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification (the international security standard), control A.8.29 (security testing in development and acceptance) is where testing against real inputs belongs; if you report under SOC 2 (an outside audit report on how a service company protects data), criterion CC8.1 covers how changes are designed, tested and approved. Contract tests that run on every change, with their results kept, are the kind of record both look for, so build them in from the first version rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your shop's checkout asks a courier company's computers for a delivery price. Every unit test uses a stand-in courier that answers {"price": 4.50}. Last month the courier began answering in pence, {"price": 450}, as its new documentation says. Your tests are all green at 92% coverage, and last night 31 customers were charged 450 pounds for delivery. A colleague says the answer is 100% coverage. What went wrong, and what would you do?

keyIdeas.idea: The stand-in answered what its author assumed, so no test ever saw the courier's real, changed format
Coverage counts lines run, not inputs tried, so 100% would still be green
Add contract tests on the courier's real responses, and validate the price instead of trusting it

recall.model: The stand-in courier answered the way its author assumed the real one would, in pounds, so no test ever saw the courier's new format in pence. Coverage counts the lines run, not the inputs tried: the line that reads the price was already covered, so 100% would still be green and the customers would still be charged 450 pounds. I'd add contract tests: keep recorded responses from the courier's real system, run our code on them on every change, and record them again whenever the courier changes its documentation. I'd also validate the price as it comes in, and reject a delivery price far outside the usual range for a person to check, instead of charging it. Then refund the 31 customers.

recall.prompt: The parser keeps the first 8 characters of every id, and the new scanners send 9 digits. Which test is most likely to catch this before it reaches the lab?
options: A unit test that runs the parser on FakeScanner's 26100514
A contract test that runs the parser on recorded reads from each real scanner model
Raising unit test coverage from 70% to 95%
recall.why: Only the contract test gives the parser what a real new scanner sends: 261005100 comes back as 26100510, and it fails at once (2 of 4 in the sim). The fake never sends 9 digits, more coverage runs more lines with the same input, and the two end-to-end samples don't collide, so they pass.

recall.prompt: Which shape of test suite does the test pyramid usually recommend?
options: Mostly end-to-end tests, because they test what users see
Equal numbers of unit, integration and end-to-end tests
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests
Only unit tests, with coverage as close to 100% as possible
recall.why: Small tests are fast and cheap to keep, so you can have many and run them on every change. Each level up runs more real parts, so it is slower and breaks more easily; Fowler calls end-to-end tests through the screens brittle, expensive to write and time consuming to run. So: many at the bottom, a few at the top.

recall.prompt: A team's unit tests reach 95% coverage, and every one of them uses the same fake scanner. What does the 95% tell you?
options: That 95% of the possible inputs have been tried
That 95% of the lines ran at least once during the tests
That the code will fail on at most 5% of real scans
That the fake scanner matches the real scanners
recall.why: Coverage counts lines run, nothing more. With one fake input, every line can run and still never meet a 9-digit id. In the sim, 21 tests at 95% are all green while 26100510 holds two cases.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The whole-id parser and the contract tests have held all winter: no id in two cases. The 10-digit spring model was refused in its contract tests, as planned, and Wolfram taught the parser 10 digits before it arrived. But in March the old scanners got a software update from the scanner company. They still read the old 8-digit tubes brought out of storage for re-testing, and since then about one in ten is refused. The screen shows the refused id as " 26100517": the update puts a space in front. The contract tests are green. Their recorded reads were made in October.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are the contract tests green while real tubes are refused, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The recordings are stale: they show the old scanner before its update, so the tests check a machine that no longer exists
Recording again must be part of every change to a scanner, its software or its labels
The refusal did its job; decide on purpose how to handle the space and add that read to the tests

coldCase.model: The contract tests are green because their recordings are stale: they were made in October, before the update, so they check an old scanner that no longer exists. A contract test is only as good as its last recording. The refusal worked, though: the new format was loud, not silent, and nothing was filed under a wrong id. Now decide on purpose what to do with the leading space: strip the space in one named step before the id is checked, and keep refusing anything else odd. Then record again from an updated old scanner, add that read to the contract tests, and make recording again part of every update to a scanner, its software or its labels, before it goes onto a bench.
